newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Oil markets calm as Saudi signals OPEC rollover.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Oil markets calm as Saudi signals OPEC rollover.

text.p: Oil markets barely flinched on Tuesday as Saudi Arabia signalled current OPEC production limits should be renewed, as expected, despite flagrant quota-busting.

Oil traders said comments from Saudi Arabian oil minister Ali bin Ibrahim al-Naimi, in Vienna for the bi-annual meeting of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries, were in line with market predictions.

"They are not saying enough to move the market at the moment," said Leslie Nicholas, energy analyst at broker GNI. "The market really expects this kind of standard PR from OPEC. We've got to have something more meaningful for them to sit up and take notice."

The remarks by Naimi and other OPEC ministers were seen as indicating the official meeting starting on Wednesday would do little to bolster oil prices, which have slumped from close to $25 last year to around $18 now for a barrel of North Sea Brent blend crude.
At 1128 GMT benchmark Brent blend futures for August were up seven cents at $18.05 a barrel.

They rose strongly on Monday on fears a U.N. resolution threatening Iraq with sanctions for blocking arms inspectors, and Baghdad's angry response, would lead to a summer of tension that would hit crude supplies.
"Ahead of the full (OPEC) ministerial meeting there is still more market attention on Iraq," Nicholas said.
The war of words continued on Tuesday with one of Baghdad's most influential newspapers predicting further friction between Iraq and U.N. arms inspectors.

Naimi said demand for oil was strong enough to soak up OPEC output, currently running two million barrels per day (bpd) above the nominal ceiling of 25.03 million bpd, and to stop prices falling further.
"Demand is good. There is no reason for prices to go lower," said Naimi, who also indicated the energetic over-production of other cartel members would be addressed.
"A rollover is good if everyone adheres to their quota," he said.
Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil exporter, and at eight million bpd the biggest quota holder, is one of the cartel's most restrained producers, despite having two million bpd in spare capacity.
It has given no hint it will abandon its stance and agree to the suggestion of cash-hungry Venezuela, that quotas should be abandoned and price ignored in a dash for market share.
Other OPEC members have called on quota violators to adhere to official allocations.
"Everything depends on the violations. Any decisions without stopping the violations does not pay," Iranian oil minister Gholamreza Aghazadeh told reporters in Vienna.
But market players doubt the cartel's ability to discipline the recalcitrant and see production continuing at around current levels.

Prices are more likely to be buoyed by fresh delays to the resumption of Iraqi crude exports, which are allowed under an oil-for-food deal with the U.N., but are now caught up in the dispute between Baghdad and the Security Council.

Iraq exported $2 billion worth of oil in the six months from December. It is entitled to start shipping out the same amount but has delayed doing so in irritation at the U.N.'s failure to release profits from the last deal to buy food.
